newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's boom needs more skills - state agency.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's boom needs more skills - state agency.

text.p: Irish state industrial development agency IDA Ireland said on Wednesday that the country needed to produce more skilled people to satisfy the record number of foreign companies creating jobs in the booming economy.
"It is fundamental to the competitiveness of this country that we upskill ourselves at every opporunity," IDA chief executive Kieran McGowan told a news conference to launch its 1996 annual report.
IDA chairman Denis Hanrahan said providing multinational firms with a supply of people with the skills, qualifications and training to carry out their plans was the biggest challenge facing the IDA.
This was "the single most important item that will determine the continued success of inward investment in future years", the IDA said in a statement.

"But it will not happen without the concerted efforts of everyone involved," said Hanrahan, appealing to government departments and agencies, educational bodies and industrial associations to cooperate to provide the education.

Ireland is undergoing an economic boom based on strong growth in which multinational companies attracted by a skilled English-speaking worforce have played a major part by creating around 1,000 jobs a week in the past two years.

IDA officials played down media talk of a "skills crisis" and said the country had succesfully adapted to the demands of a changing investment climate in the past and would continue to do so in the future.
The IDA said that Ireland ranked second behind Singapore in a recent world competitiveness report published in Lausanne on education systems.
"It will be important to continue achieving this high ranking and to do so by being responsive and flexible to the changing needs of business as they arise," Hanrahan said.
Ireland now ranks as the most-favoured "Greenfield Site" for U.S. companies setting up abroad, especially in the hi-tech, electronics and computer sectors, the IDA says.
McGowan said Ireland was not unique and many U.S. computer companies he spoke to complained of a skills shortage in every potential location.
He cited Seagate Technology and Hewlett Packard, U.S. companies which have both announced major projects in Ireland in the past few weeks.
"They made the point very strongly that every country has shortages and feel we are handling situation better than in other countries," McGowan said.

He said he hoped that 1997 would match "and perhaps do a little better" than 1996 in attracing foreign companies and forecast growth for the services and medical equipment sector as well as traditional hi-tech areas.
Last year was the third consecutive year of record job creation with 206 projects creating 13,319 jobs.

The 1,000 IDA-backed companies now operating in Ireland are worth in excess of 5.7 billion pounds annually to the economy with exchequer and tax revenues exceeding 10 million pounds a week, the IDA said.
